EC2 CLC Data Analysis

AMP

2026-02-25

Coastal Land Conversion Project

Rationale: to look at more localized drivers of VRR based on Molino et al., 2023 hypothesis that these are dependent on local drivers. https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2023JG007525

Datasets:

  1. vertical retreat rate

Dataset from: Chen and Kirwan 2023 https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gcb.17081 - vertical forest retreat rates for every point along the mid-Atlantic https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=knb-lter-vcr.399.1

  1. threshold elevations

Dataset from: Molino et al 2022 https://aslopubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/lol2.10262 - threshold elevation defining the boundary between forest and marsh, aggregated by watershed. This is only for Maryland and Virginia, so won’t work for EXCHANGE sites in DE or NJ https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=knb-lter-vcr.343.2

  1. Watershed parameters from Molino et al 2022

  2. Soil parameters from EC1 v3

https://data.ess-dive.lbl.gov/view/doi%3A10.15485%2F1960313

Analysis to be completed in this script:

  1. Multiple linear regression of vertical retreat rate vs. EC1 soil parameters

  2. Multiple linear regression of threshold elevations vs. EC1 soil parameters (+ identified watershed parameters from Molino et al)

For WRT: α is a scale parameter that is inversely proportional to the mean pore diameter; n is a shape parameter that controls the slope of the soil-water characteristic curve; θr is the residual water content, and θs is the saturated water content.

This subset of samples has a better overall model fit (R2=0.7) than all the watersheds in the original study (R2 = 0.5ish) but the relative importance of the 3 variables from the Molino paper are weaker than in the manuscript.

Strongest relationships are local surface water salinity and theta - positive relationship with surface water salinity means higher threshold elevations with higher salinity. I wonder if this related at all to slope, because I would hypothesize this relationship would be negative (ie. high salinity = more salt stress, equals lower elevation of marsh conversion) - negative relationship with theta means at sites with higher saturated water content (soil) in the upland soils have lower threshold elevations, which means more water can get into (and stay?) the soils during flooding.

To address the research question, Can local site characteristics improve predictions of watershed-scale forest retreat (explain previously unexplained variance)?

use leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) to confirm macro-scale dominance in the subset of samples

loocv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  n <- nrow(data)
  preds <- numeric(n)
  
  for (i in 1:n) {
    train <- data[-i, ]
    test  <- data[i, , drop = FALSE]
    
    fit <- lm(formula, data = train)
    preds[i] <- predict(fit, newdata = test)
  }
  
  sqrt(mean((data$Elevation - preds)^2))
}


rmse_macro <- loocv_rmse(Elevation ~ Surface_Salinity, clc_mlr)
rmse_micro <- loocv_rmse(Elevation ~ th_s + alpha, clc_mlr)
rmse_combo <- loocv_rmse(Elevation ~ Surface_Salinity + th_s + alpha, clc_mlr)

rmse_macro
